messages.text: What are the emergency warning signs of severe dengue that require immediate hospitalization?

According to the World Health Organization (WHO Fact Sheets on Dengue & Severe Dengue): Warning signs typically appear 3 to 7 days after the first symptoms, often as fever drops. These include persistent vomiting (more than 3 times in 24 hours), severe abdominal pain, fluid accumulation with respiratory difficulty, mucosal bleeding (gums or nose), blood in vomit or stools, and extreme restlessness or lethargy. Any patient exhibiting these warning signs requires immediate emergency hospitalization.
messages.spoken_text: Warning signs of severe dengue include persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, fluid accumulation, bleeding, and extreme lethargy. Patients showing any warning sign must be hospitalized immediately.

documents.title: WHO Fact Sheets & Prevention Guidelines: Dengue, Severe Dengue, and Malaria
documents.publisher: World Health Organization (WHO) & Global Health Observatory
documents.reviewer_name: Dr. V. Ramanathan (Vector-Borne Diseases & Public Health Analyst)
documents.summary: Clinical presentation of dengue and malaria, critical warning signs of severe dengue, when to seek emergency hospital care, and vector prevention methods.

chunks.title: Symptoms of Dengue and Malaria and How to Differentiate Them
chunks.text: Dengue typically manifests with high sudden fever (40°C/104°F) accompanied by at least two symptoms: severe frontal headache, intense pain behind the eyes (retro-orbital pain), muscle and joint pains (breakbone fever), nausea, vomiting, swollen glands, and macular rash. Malaria, transmitted by night-biting Anopheles mosquitoes, presents with paroxysms of high fever preceded by violent chills and rigors, followed by profuse drenching sweats, fatigue, and jaundice.

chunks.title: Severe Dengue Warning Signs: When to Seek Immediate Hospital Care
chunks.text: Severe dengue is a life-threatening medical emergency due to plasma leakage, fluid accumulation, respiratory distress, severe bleeding, or organ impairment. Warning signs typically appear 3 to 7 days after first symptoms, often as fever drops: persistent vomiting (more than 3 times in 24 hours), severe abdominal pain, rapid breathing, bleeding gums or nose, blood in vomit or stools, and extreme lethargy or restlessness. Patients showing any warning sign must be hospitalized immediately.

chunks.title: Vector Control and Personal Prevention Guidelines
chunks.text: The primary mosquito vector for dengue, Aedes aegypti, bites primarily during daytime (early morning and late afternoon) and breeds in domestic standing water. Prevention requires: 1) Emptying, scrubbing, and covering water storage containers, flower vases, and discarded tyres weekly; 2) Using insect repellent containing DEET, Picaridin, or IR3535 on exposed skin; 3) Wearing long-sleeved light-colored clothing; and 4) Sleeping under insecticide-treated bed nets (ITNs) to prevent nocturnal malaria transmission.

documents.title: WHO Child Growth Standards: Guidelines for Growth Assessment and Monitoring
documents.reviewer_name: Dr. K. Jayasree (Pediatrician & Child Growth Standards Specialist)
documents.summary: Interpretation principles for WHO Child Growth Standards (length/height-for-age, weight-for-age, BMI-for-age), z-scores, and longitudinal growth tracking boundaries.

chunks.title: Principles and Foundation of the WHO Child Growth Standards
chunks.text: The WHO Child Growth Standards establish how children worldwide should grow under optimal nutritional, environmental, and healthcare conditions. Developed from the Multicentre Growth Reference Study (MGRS) across six countries, the standards demonstrate that healthy breastfed children from diverse ethnic backgrounds follow identical physiological growth patterns when raised in supportive environments.

chunks.title: Interpreting Growth Curves and Z-Scores: Screening Principles
chunks.text: Growth charts use standard deviation scores (z-scores) relative to the median. Measurements between -2 and +2 z-scores (3rd to 97th percentiles) encompass normal healthy biological variation. A single plotted point is a screening indicator, not a clinical diagnosis. Health professionals evaluate the growth trajectory over successive monthly visits: crossing two or more major percentile lines downward indicates growth faltering, warranting clinical dietary and developmental evaluation.

chunks.title: Understanding Stunting, Wasting, and When to Seek Pediatric Care
chunks.text: Stunting (length/height-for-age below -2 z-scores) reflects chronic undernutrition and frequent infections. Wasting (weight-for-length/height below -2 z-scores) indicates acute, severe nutritional deficit requiring urgent supplemental feeding and medical attention. If a child stops gaining weight, shows persistent lack of energy, or crosses below -2 z-scores, consult an accredited pediatrician or anganwadi nutrition worker for tailored clinical assessment.

documents.title: PAHO / WHO Educational Guide: Managing Fever and Common Symptoms Safely
documents.jurisdiction: Pan American (PAHO IRIS) & WHO Global Guidelines
documents.reviewer_name: Dr. E. Gomez & Dr. R. Sundaram (Clinical Emergency Reviewers)
documents.summary: Evidence-based understanding of acute fever, home comfort measures, safe hydration, explicit boundary against self-diagnosis, and critical danger signs.

chunks.title: Understanding Fever as a Physiological Response and Home Care
chunks.text: Fever is an elevated body temperature (above 38.0°C or 100.4°F) that serves as the body's natural defense mechanism to fight viral or bacterial pathogens. Basic supportive home care includes: offering ample fluids (clean water, oral rehydration solutions, soups) to prevent dehydration, dressing in lightweight breathable cotton clothing, and keeping room temperature comfortable. Sponging with cold water or alcohol is strictly unsafe and discouraged.

chunks.title: Red Flag Symptoms: When Fever Requires Immediate Emergency Evaluation
chunks.text: Seek immediate emergency medical care if fever is accompanied by: 1) Any fever in an infant under 3 months old; 2) Stiff neck, inability to touch chin to chest, or intense light sensitivity (photophobia); 3) New pinpoint red-purple spots on the skin that do not fade when pressed (petechial rash); 4) Difficulty breathing, rapid grunting respirations; 5) Inconsolable crying, extreme drowsiness, or inability to wake up; or 6) Febrile seizures or confusion.

chunks.title: Preparing Questions for Your Doctor Regarding Fever and Symptoms
chunks.text: Before visiting your doctor, maintain a temperature log noting when fever peaks, fluid intake, urine frequency, and associated symptoms like cough or vomiting. When meeting your clinician, ask: 1) What is the suspected cause of this fever? 2) How many days should we expect it to last? 3) Exactly what red flags would require us to return to the emergency room? 4) What is the safe, age-appropriate dosage for fever relief if discomfort persists?

documents.title: Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY & ABHA Health Account Official Guidelines (with WHO UHC Context)
documents.publisher: National Health Authority (NHA), myScheme India & WHO Universal Health Coverage (UHC)
documents.jurisdiction: India (National) / WHO Universal Health Coverage Alignment
documents.reviewer_name: Rajesh Sharma & WHO Health Financing Team (Policy Analysts)
documents.license_notes: Government of India Open Data License & WHO UHC Partnership
documents.summary: Eligibility criteria, ₹5 lakh health cover, cashless hospitalization, ABHA account creation, required documents, and WHO UHC financial protection context.

chunks.title: Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY Benefits, ₹5 Lakh Cover, and WHO UHC Context
chunks.text: Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB PM-JAY) is aligned with WHO Universal Health Coverage (UHC) goals to shield vulnerable populations from catastrophic healthcare expenditures. The scheme provides a defined health benefit cover of up to ₹5,00,000 (Five Lakh Rupees) per eligible family per year for secondary and tertiary care hospitalization. The scheme is completely cashless and paperless at all empaneled public and private healthcare facilities nationwide.

chunks.title: Eligibility Verification: SECC 2011 and Official Search Portals
chunks.text: PM-JAY eligibility is pre-determined based on Socio-Economic and Caste Census (SECC 2011) deprivation criteria for rural households (categories D1 to D7) and occupational categories for urban households. Citizens can verify eligibility without fees by: 1) Searching the official portal at mera.pmjay.gov.in; 2) Calling the national toll-free helpline 14555; or 3) Meeting an Ayushman Mitra stationed at any empaneled hospital.

chunks.title: Mandatory Documents Required to Generate Ayushman Card
chunks.text: To generate the Ayushman Card (Golden Card) and receive cashless admission, beneficiaries must present: 1) Government photo identity proof (Aadhaar Card or approved government photo ID); 2) Proof of family identification (Ration Card, PM letter, or State Family ID); and 3) An active mobile phone for OTP verification. Generating the Ayushman Card at Common Service Centres (CSCs) or public hospitals is completely free of cost.

chunks.title: Creating an ABHA (Ayushman Bharat Health Account) Digital ID
chunks.section: Digital Health Mission & Health Records — Clause 5.1
chunks.text: The Ayushman Bharat Health Account (ABHA) is a unique 14-digit digital health identification under the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM). Any citizen can create their ABHA number free in minutes at healthid.ndhm.gov.in or through the ABHA mobile app using Aadhaar or driving license. ABHA facilitates secure, consent-based digital storage and sharing of diagnostic lab reports and medical prescriptions across participating hospitals.

documents.title: WHO Guidelines on Diagnosis and Management of Type 2 Diabetes
documents.reviewer_name: Dr. S. K. Rao (Consultant Diabetologist & Clinical Reviewer)
documents.summary: Evidence-based guidance on dietary management, HbA1c monitoring, regular physical activity, and identification of hypoglycemia.

chunks.title: Dietary Habits and Blood Sugar Control in Type 2 Diabetes
chunks.text: A balanced diet rich in dietary fiber—including whole grains, legumes, pulses, vegetables, and low-glycemic fruits—helps moderate postprandial glucose surges. Highly refined carbohydrates, sweetened beverages, and ultra-processed foods should be restricted. Spacing meals consistently throughout the day prevents acute swings in blood sugar.

chunks.title: Physical Activity Recommendations for Adults with Diabetes
chunks.text: Adults with type 2 diabetes are advised to engage in at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity per week, such as brisk walking, cycling, or swimming, spread over at least 3 days with no more than two consecutive days without exercise. Muscle-strengthening activities 2 to 3 days weekly provide additional insulin-sensitizing benefits.

chunks.title: Recognizing Hypoglycemia (Low Blood Sugar) and Immediate Care
chunks.text: Hypoglycemia occurs when blood glucose drops below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L). Early symptoms include cold shakiness, sweating, palpitations, sudden hunger, dizziness, and irritability. Immediate self-care involves the "Rule of 15": ingest 15 grams of fast-acting glucose (e.g., 3-4 glucose tablets, half a cup of fruit juice, or 3 teaspoons of sugar in water), rest for 15 minutes, and re-check blood sugar. If confusion or loss of consciousness occurs, seek immediate emergency care.

documents.title: WHO/UNICEF Infant and Young Child Feeding & Maternal Care Guidelines
documents.reviewer_name: Dr. P. Anitha (Maternal & Child Health Specialist)
documents.summary: Exclusive breastfeeding standards, complementary feeding introduction, and maternal postpartum red flags.

chunks.title: Exclusive Breastfeeding in the First 6 Months of Life
chunks.text: WHO and UNICEF universally recommend exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months (180 days) of life. Exclusive breastfeeding means the infant receives only breast milk without additional food, water, tea, or formula, with exceptions only for necessary oral rehydration solution, vitamin/mineral drops, or doctor-prescribed medicine.

documents.title: WHO Guideline for the Treatment of Hypertension
documents.summary: Blood pressure benchmarks, dietary sodium reduction, regular monitoring, and lifestyle modifications.

chunks.title: Understanding Blood Pressure Readings and Thresholds
chunks.text: Blood pressure is recorded as systolic over diastolic in mmHg. Normal resting blood pressure is generally under 120/80 mmHg. Hypertension is diagnosed when systolic blood pressure is persistently 140 mmHg or higher and/or diastolic is 90 mmHg or higher across two clinical measurements.

chunks.title: Dietary Sodium Reduction for High Blood Pressure
chunks.text: WHO strongly recommends reducing daily salt intake to less than 5 grams per day (under 2 grams of sodium, or about 1 level teaspoon of salt). High dietary sodium stiffens blood vessels and elevates pressure. Concurrently increasing dietary potassium through natural foods lowers cardiovascular strain.
